title: Salicylic acid for acne
content: Salicylic acid is commonly used in acne care because it exfoliates the skin and helps open clogged pores. It is especially useful for blackheads and whiteheads. Acne products can still cause dryness or irritation, so a gentle routine and moisturizer can be helpful.

title: Benzoyl peroxide for acne
content: Benzoyl peroxide is an acne-fighting ingredient that reduces acne-causing bacteria on the skin. It is often combined with treatments that target other causes of acne. Lower-strength products may be easier to tolerate because dryness and irritation can occur.

title: Azelaic acid
content: Azelaic acid has anti-inflammatory properties and is used for mild to moderate acne. It can help with clogged pores, acne-related inflammation, and post-inflammatory dark marks. Sensitive skin may still experience irritation, redness, scaling, itching, or burning.

title: Niacinamide (nicotinamide)
content: Niacinamide, also called nicotinamide, is a form of vitamin B3 used in many topical skincare products. Evidence described by DermNet suggests it can support skin barrier function, reduce water loss, improve hydration, and may help acne through anti-inflammatory effects and reduced sebum production. It is generally well tolerated topically.

title: Topical retinoids
content: Topical retinoids are vitamin A-derived medications used for acne and photoaging. They can help unclog pores and improve comedonal and inflammatory acne. Dryness and sun sensitivity can occur, so daytime sun protection and moisturizer are commonly recommended. Some retinoids are prescription medicines depending on the country and product.

title: Hyaluronic acid and dry skin
content: Hyaluronic acid is a humectant used in moisturizers to help hydrate the skin. The American Academy of Dermatology lists hyaluronic acid among useful moisturizing ingredients and recommends fragrance-free moisturizers for people with dry or sensitive skin when possible.

title: Ceramides and the skin barrier
content: Ceramides are lipid molecules found in moisturizers that can help support hydration and moisture retention. They are among ingredients dermatologists commonly recommend looking for in moisturizers, particularly when the skin is dry or the barrier is stressed.

title: Sunscreen basics
content: Dermatologists recommend broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher as part of daily sun protection. Sun protection also includes seeking shade and wearing protective clothing. Sunscreen is important for reducing UV-related skin damage and is a foundational part of many skincare routines.

title: Basic skincare product order
content: A simple skincare order recommended by dermatologists is: cleanse first, then apply medication or treatment if used, then moisturizer and/or sunscreen, and makeup last if desired. Using too many products at once can irritate the skin.

title: Vitamin C in skincare
content: Vitamin C is an antioxidant used in skincare and is commonly included in products intended to brighten the appearance of skin. It is one of several optional active ingredients and does not replace foundational steps such as moisturizer and sunscreen.

title: Fragrance and sensitive or dry skin
content: Fragrance can irritate some people with dry or sensitive skin and can sometimes trigger allergic skin reactions. Dermatologists often recommend fragrance-free products when irritation is a concern.

title: Acne-friendly moisturizer
content: People with acne may still benefit from moisturizer, especially when acne treatments cause dryness. Labels such as oil-free, non-comedogenic, or won't clog pores can help identify moisturizers less likely to contribute to breakouts. Applying moisturizer after washing can help retain water in the skin.
